utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we start with the next witness, a few procedural matters. I'll try to go through them as quickly as possible. First, I'd like to put on the record that the Chamber has not been sitting on the 2nd to the 4th of September, because the Gotovina Defence had informally withdrawn Witness Pokaz. Then I'd like to move into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber still has to deliver its reasons for the -- for a Prosecution request in relation to Witness Sterc. These are the Chamber's reasons for its decision to strike paragraphs 3, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, and 7 from Witness Sterc's Rule 92 ter statement and admit the remaining parts of the statement into evidence. On 9 July 2009, the Gotovina Defence submitted a Rule 92 ter statement for Witness Sterc. On the same day, the Prosecution filed an objection to the statement, arguing that portions of the statement were, in substance, an expert report which should have been tendered pursuant to Rule 94 bis and that it had not received proper disclosure of underlying documents to be able to assess the witness's opinions, and for these reasons the Prosecution requested that paragraphs 3, 5, and 7 of the statement be stricken, or, alternatively, that the Prosecution be provided adequate time to prepare for cross-examination following disclosure of the underlying documents. The matter was also addressed in court that day and was the subject of informal communications between the parties and the Chamber on the 10th of July, 2009. On the 14th of July, the Rule 92 ter statement was orally tendered into evidence and subsequently marked for identification as D1607. This can be found at transcript pages 20.260. On the 15th of July, 2009, the Chamber partially admitted Witness Sterc's Rule 92 ter statement, excluding paragraphs 3, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, and 7. This decision can be found at transcript pages 20.343 and 20.344. The Chamber previously considered that parties are not necessarily precluded from eliciting opinions from fact witnesses, that clear lines cannot always be drawn between fact and opinion and very simple statements can also include elements of both. When a fact witness offers an opinion as part of his testimony, the Chamber considers whether that opinion has a factual basis in what the witness has personally experienced, and whether the witness needed any special knowledge, experience, or skills in order to substantiate it. In determining whether a piece of evidence can be admitted, the Chamber further considers whether the evidence predominantly consists of opinions or facts. However, when a witness provides opinions or conclusions that are of an expert character, that is, they require that the person providing them has some sort of specialised knowledge, skill, or training, the Chamber expects this witness to provide this expert opinion in full transparency of the established or assumed facts he or she relies upon and of the methods used when applying his or her knowledge, experience, or skills to form his or her expert opinion. Whenever possible, the parties should be given the opportunity to test or challenge the factual basis and methodology on which the expert has reached his or her conclusions. Moreover, a minimum degree of transparency in the sources and methods used in an expert report is required at the stage of admission into evidence in order for the Chamber to determine the report's probative value. The Chamber should be satisfied that the expert witness has at his or her disposal the special knowledge, experience, or skills needed to potentially assist the Chamber to understand or determine issues in dispute. The fulfilment of these requirements is usually ensured through the mechanisms of Rule 94 bis of the Rules. In the present case, the witness was not proposed by the Gotovina Defence pursuant to this Rule. The Chamber considered paragraphs 3, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, and 7 of Witness Sterc's Rule 92 ter statement, which described the results of demographic and scientific analysis and contain further conclusions that were drawn on the basis of these results, to be of an expert character. In order to prevent expert testimony being presented under the guise of a witness of fact, the Chamber expects the evidence presented by Witness Sterc to meet the requirements which apply in relation to expert witnesses set out above. However, the Chamber found that, in the present case, the opinions and conclusions of Witness Sterc were not provided in full transparency of the established or assumed facts he relied upon and of the methods he used to form these opinions and conclusions. Consequently, the Chamber found that the parties were not in a position to explore the basis on which Witness Sterc reached these conclusions and the Chamber was not in a position to adequately assess the probative value of these portions of the witness's 92 ter statements. Paragraphs 3, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, and 7 of Witness Sterc's Rule 92 ter statement were therefore not admitted into evidence. The Chamber was satisfied that the remains parts of Witness Sterc's witness statement are relevant and of probative value and could be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter (A) of the Rules. For these reasons, the Chamber decided to partially admit Witness Sterc's Rule 92 ter statement into evidence, excluding paragraphs 3, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4 and 7. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision on the admission of the Rule 92 ter statement for Witness Sterc. The Chamber also has to give the reasons for the decision on the Prosecution's objection to the Barkovic Rule 92 ter statement. These are the Chamber's reasons for denying the Prosecution's objection to the Gotovina Defence's submission of the Rule 92 ter statement of Witness Barkovic. On the 10th of June, 2009, the Gotovina Defence submitted a Rule 92 ter statement for Witness Barkovic. On the 23rd of June, the Prosecution filed an objection to the statement, requesting both that a portion of the statement be stricken and that the witness be precluded from testifying as an expert on certain matters, due to lack of qualifications. On the 25th of June, 2009, the Gotovina Defence requested leave to reply. The Chamber granted the request and informed the parties accordingly through an informal communication on the 29th of June, 2009. The Gotovina Defence's reply, filed on the 30th of June, 2009, asserted that the testimony would focus on facts, not on expert opinions and that the witness had sufficient experience in the relevant field to provide a factual basis for his statements. Additionally, the reply cited an earlier decision from this case, which held that there was no need for an order preventing the Prosecution from seeking opinions from a fact witness. This decision can be found at transcript pages 1927 through 1929. In court on the 9th of July, 2009, the Chamber denied both the Prosecution's objection to the admission of portions of the statement and its request to prevent the witness from testifying on certain matters. This decision can be found at transcript page 20.117. In the decision cited by the Gotovina Defence, the Chamber noted that, although the testimony of any witness might contain opinions, the parties have sufficient opportunity to challenge these in court and are instructed to explore their factual basis. The Chamber remains mindful of this reasoning. Clear lines cannot always be drawn between fact and opinion, and very simple statements can also include elements of both. As the Chamber has already set out in its reasons for its decision to strike paragraphs 3, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, and 7 from Witness Sterc's Rule 92 ter statement, when a fact witness offers an opinion as part of his testimony, the Chamber considers whether that opinion has a factual basis in what the witness has personally experienced. When a witness provides opinions or conclusions which are of an expert character, the Chamber expects this witness to provide its expert opinion in full transparency of the established or assumed facts he or she relies upon and of the methods used when applying his or her specialized knowledge, experience, or skills to form his or her expert opinion. In determining whether a piece of evidence can be admitted, the Chamber further considers whether the evidence predominantly consists of opinions or facts. In the present case, the Chamber was satisfied that in Witness Barkovic's 92 ter statement where he described having worked for several years in the field that was the subject of his testimony, the witness focuses on facts, not opinions of an expert character, and that the statement concerns his own experience and observations. The Chamber concluded that the factual bases for the challenged portions of Witness Barkovic's statement and oral testimony could be explored sufficiently with reference to his personal experiences, and that the conclusions were not of a kind to require some specialised knowledge, skill or training, and for these reasons, the Prosecution's request -- should say requests to strike parts of the witness statement and to limit the scope of his testimony were denied. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision on the Prosecution's objection to the Rule 92 ter statement for Witness Barkovic. The last decision to be delivered is the Chamber's decision on the admission into evidence of Exhibit P2593. On the 17th of July, 2009, during the cross-examination of Witness Sterc, the Prosecution tendered into evidence the transcript of a meeting between members of the Croatian leadership on, amongst other matters, the reintegration of Serbs into Eastern Slavonia. The Gotovina Defence objected to the admission into evidence of the document. The Chamber subsequently invited the parties to make further submissions on the issue. This can be found at transcript pages 20.433 to 20.437. On the 20th of July, 2009, both the Gotovina Defence and the Prosecution filed further submissions. Neither the Cermak Defence nor the Markac Defence made any submissions. In its submissions, the Gotovina Defence argues that the Prosecution failed to comply with its obligations under Rule 90(H)(ii) of the Rules to introduce the document P2593 during cross-examination of Witness Skare Ozbolt, who, unlike Witness Sterc, was present at the meeting that P2593 transcribes. It argues that the document should therefore not be admitted into evidence. The Prosecution submits that P2593 is relevant to, and of probative value on, the views of members of the Croatian leadership on the desirability of a largely ethnically homogeneous Croatia. It further submits that, by putting its case on this matter to Witness Skare Ozbolt, it had fulfilled its obligations under Rule 90(H)(ii) of the Rules during cross-examination of this witness. Rule 90(H)(ii) of the Rules provides as follows, and I quote: "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." In its Judgement in the case of Momcilo Krajisnik, the Appeals Chamber explained that this rule seeks to facilitate the fair and efficient presentation of evidence whilst affording the witness being cross-examined the possibility of explaining himself on those aspects of his testimony, contradicted by the opposing parties' evidence. This would saving the witness from having to reappear needlessly in order to explain him or herself and would enable the Trial Chamber to evaluate the credibility of the testimony more accurately. The Appeals Chamber concluded that in order to fulfil the requirements of this rule, it is sufficient that the cross-examining party puts to the witness the general substance of its case conflicting with the evidence of the witness. In the present case, the Prosecution put to Witness Skare Ozbolt various documents, apparently aiming to show that the policy of the Croatian leadership was to minimise the number of Serbs in Eastern Slavonia and the Krajina region, and that their primary concern was to permanently settle Croats in these areas. This can be found at transcript pages 18.148 to 18.165; at pages 18.188 to 18.196; and at pages 18.202 to 18.212. The Chamber therefore considers that Witness Skare Ozbolt had sufficient opportunity to explain herself on those aspects of her testimony relating to the policy of the Croatian leadership with regard to Eastern Slavonia which were contradicted by the Prosecution's evidence. In the Krajisnik Appeals Judgement, the Appeals Chamber moreover found that there is no need under Rule 90(H)(ii) for the cross-examining party to explain every detail of the contradictory evidence and that the rule allows for some flexibility depending on the circumstances of the trial. Consequently, the Chamber finds that there is no obligation under Rule 90(H)(ii) for the cross-examining party to put to the witness all documents or any specific document which might relate to a witness's evidence which is contradictory to a party's case. Considering this, and in view of the purpose of the Rule, the Chamber finds that the Prosecution has, in this case, not breached its obligation under Rule 90(H)(ii). Notwithstanding this, the Chamber reiterates that it is best assisted if documents are tendered in a meaningful way through witnesses who are in a position to provide the best possible contextualisation. The Chamber proceeds to consider whether the document meets the requirements for admission into evidence under Rule 89 (C) of the Rules, that is, whether the documents are relevant and of probative value. No argument was advanced by the Gotovina Defence challenging either the relevance or the probative value of the document. P2593 is the transcript of a meeting between members of the Croatian leadership, including persons who allegedly were members of the alleged joint criminal enterprise, which could provide an insight into their views and policies relating to the return of Serbs to Croatia and on issues related to the re-integration of Serbs. While noting that the territorial scope of the indictment is not focussing on Eastern Slavonia but, rather, the municipalities listed in Counts 1 through 9, the Chamber is satisfied that Operation Storm cannot be viewed in temporal or geographical isolation but forms an episode in a continuum and the document is relevant and of probative value. The Chamber hereby admits document P2593 into evidence. The Chamber notes that the English translation of the exhibit is missing the cover page included in the B/C/S original, and therefore, instructs the Prosecution to add the missing page to the English translation and to notify the Registrar, the Chamber, and the parties when this has been done. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the admission into evidence of P2593. The Chamber would like to put on the record that an extra session has been scheduled for the afternoon of Friday, the 11th of September, in order to finish the testimony of witness Corn before the weekend. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution's objections to the use of certain documents with Witness Corn, focussing on three documents, has become moot because the Gotovina Defence does not intend to use those documents anymore.

utterances.text: Good morning, Professor. Professor, can you state your name for the record and spell your last name.

utterances.text: Geoffrey S. Corn. Last name is spelled C-o-r-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the ease of moving through this testimony I've provided the Registrar with a hard copy of some of these documents, so if we can -- with the Court's permission if he could be given that binder.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: This is my curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir ... Professor, we're not going to through everything in this curriculum vitae, but can you briefly give your qualifications as well as your education and military training to the Trial Chamber, sir.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: My civilian education began with my undergraduate bachelors of arts degree from Hartwick College in Oneonta, New York, which I received in 1983 with a degree -- a specialisation in history. In 1989, I began my law degree education at George Washington University. I graduated from George Washington in 1992 with a juris doctorate. I graduated highest honours with that degree, which indicates that my performance placed me in the top two per cent of my graduating class. In 1996, I attended the US Army Judge Advocate General's school. The US Army Judge Advocate General, or JAG school, is the only military school in the United States that's accredited by the American Bar Association to grant an advance degree in law. It's accredited to grant a master's of law degree, an LL.M. I was awarded the LL.M. at the end of that ten-month course of study with a specialisation in international and operational law. And I graduated from that course first in my class as distinguished graduate. My military education began when I chose to enlist in the US Army in 1993. I have been to numerous military schools. I started as a private, attended basic combat training. From there I attended US Army Officer Candidate School at Fort Benning, Georgia. It's a four-month commissioning course. I graduated as a distinguished military graduate from that course in 1984, June 1st. From there I was branched a military intelligence officer. I attended the US Army Military Intelligence Officers Basic Course at Fort Huachuca, Arizona. That's a six-month course focussed on training as a tactical intelligence officer. I returned to Fort Huachuca in 1988 to attend a six-month military intelligence officers advance course. The focus of that course is to teach you more of a specialty. At that time I specialized in a course on imagery analysis and exploitation. While I was in that course I was selected by the army to attend what's called the Funded Legal Education Programme. That's a programme the US Army offers to approximately 10 to 15 officers every year to attend law school at government expense in exchange for a commitment to serve as a Judge Advocate for six years following your graduation. It was after that selection that I attended George Washington University to earn my law degree. When I graduated from law school, I then attended the Judge Advocate General's Corps basic course in Charlottesville, Virginia, which is the initial introductory course for new JAG officers, military lawyers. I went off to my first assignment as a JAG after that. I returned to the JAG school in 1996 to attend the masters of law programme. After completing that programme I served on the faculty at the Judge Advocate General's School in the International and Operational Law Department as a professor of international operational and national security law for three years. During that time I was selected to attend the army's command and general staff college. That is not a course that is designed for military lawyers. It's a course designed primarily to teach field-grade level operations. It's attended by about 1100 officers from all the services to include about 100 international officers. Only about 15 Judge Advocate General officers are selected each year to attend that course. It is a ten-month course at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. I attended that course from 2000 -- the summer of 2000 till graduation in May of 2001, and graduated at that time. That was the last military school I attended during my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, when you use it's acronym JAG, J-A-G, I take it that you're referring to the Judge Advocate General?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: The -- the organisation in the US Army for military attorneys is called the JAG Corps, the Judge Advocate General Corps. The Judge Advocate General is the senior military lawyer for the United States Army, and the navy and air force have their own TJAG, The Judge Advocate General. But when I refer to the JAG Corps or serving as a JAG, it is synonymous with stating that I served in the capacity as a military legal advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor Corn, what rank in the military did you achieve prior to your retirement and when did you actually retire from the military?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: My official retirement date was 1 November 2004. I retired in the rank of lieutenant-colonel. I was promoted to each rank at the normal point in time, based on the statistics for the military, and that culminated in approximately 21 years of military, active military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And since that time, Professor, have you continued to work in the field of the Law of Armed Conflict and other areas involving international humanitarian law in your subsequent endeavours?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Well, in fact, when I made the decision to retire from active military service, I then applied and was selected for a position as a civilian legal advisor with the Department of the Army that. That position was in the Office of the Judge Advocate General in the international law division and I was the chief of the law of war branch. The position is also designated as the special assistant for law of war matters to the Judge Advocate General of the army. But what -- the position really was, was the army's senior law of war expert and I took that position at the -- after I retired in the fall of 2004, with the expectation that I would spend a good deal of time serving in that civilian capacity with the army. It was about halfway through that year that I was offered the opportunity to join a law faculty as a full-time professor, and I made a decision that that was what I wanted to do and I thought that it was an opportunity that might not present itself again. So it was a difficult choice, but at that time, I chose to leave government service and move to academia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I note from your curriculum vitae that, as we speak, you are an associate professor of law at South Texas College of Law.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: That's right. I have been at South Texas for a little bit more than four years. I teach criminal law, constitutional criminal procedure, the Law of Armed Conflict, comparative counter-terrorism law, and during that time, my scholarship has focussed almost exclusively on issues related to the Law of Armed Conflict, to includes a book that I've written with some colleagues, former JAG officers, that is going to be published in about two weeks, I think, by Oxford University Press, titled "The Law of War and the War on Terror."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, directing your attention to the field of artillery and can you just give a brief over view to the Trial Chamber of your knowledge and training with respect to the artillery and how your experiences qualify you to provide an expert analysis of the application of Law on Armed Conflict and the use of artillery during military operations?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Well, obviously from my discussion of my military education, I -- it's clear I never served as an artillery officer, but both in my capacity as a tactical intelligence officer and in my capacity as a military legal advisor, I had routine experiences related to the assessment and analysis of the use of artillery and artillery support in the planning and execution of planned and military operations for training and some planing involving military operations for actual combat. This really began when I started my military career as a tactical intelligence officer in Panama. I was an assistant intelligence officer in a infantry brigade, and I was the intelligence staff officer for a paratroop infantry battalion in Panama, and in that capacity you're constantly involved in the targeting process during training and preparation for operations, training both with our forces and multi-national forces all over South and Central America. The interrelationship between the tactical intelligence officer and the fire support officer is -- it's just in -- indelible connection because the fire support officer is responsive to the intelligence information that's being produced related to the tactical execution of the operation. That continued, obviously, during the military education I had. All military education in the US Army has a core component, so when you intend [sic], for example, the intelligence basic or advanced course, you begin with a ten-week core curriculum that all military officers are provided, and part of that is learning the basic aspects of the fire support system and the fire support process. I think my -- actually my understanding of fire support increased when I began serving as a JAG officer. My first assignment as a JAG was at fort Campbell, Kentucky, with the 101st Airborne Division. And while I served in that position I was the legal advisor for a brigade combat team, the 3rd Brigade combat team, and in that capacity I was the officer responsible for providing the commander advice and his staff advice on the legality of the employment of combat power during the training and execution of military operations. So I was routinely involved in targeting meetings, target assessment, target analysis, and there is a close interrelationship between the JAG and the fire support officer because, obviously, fire support missions have a significant potential for implicating compliance with the Law of Armed Conflict. That experience continued at the JAG school. One of the things we endeavoured to do was to make sure we taught student not only the law but the context in which the law would be applied. So in our education and training at the JAG school for US Army and multi-service and some international military legal advisors, they were required to gain a basic understanding of the role of fire support and the capability and effects of fire support assets that are routinely used in US military operations. And then when I went to Germany as the chief of international law for US Army Europe, one of the -- I was there from 2001 to 2003, and obviously during that time there was significant preparation for US military forces to participate in operations Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan and Iraqi Freedom in Iraq. As a matter of fact, the unit across the street from us in Heidelberg, the 5th United States Army Corps, was designated as the land force component command for Operation Iraqi Freedom in March of 2003. And we were extensively involved in the training and preparation of the JAG officers that would participate in that military operation and also in review of plans and orders related to that operation, to ensure they complied with the Law of Armed Conflict and any established policy mandates. So my interaction with the fire support system has been extensive from the beginning of my military career till the time I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going back to the document, Professor, that's on the screen, which is the -- in tab 4, which is Lieutenant-Colonel Konings's report. utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Well, this was the -- this was related to the first contact I had with the Defence team. I was asked in December of 2008 if I would be willing to review a report that had been submitted by an expert on behalf of the Prosecution, with the view of essentially critiquing it from the perspective of whether it was an accurate or effective explanation of the law, as it related to the employment of indirect fire artillery. So I was provided with this report, and so obviously my first step in this process was to do my own self-assessment of the report. And as I read through the report, I became convinced that the report included a substantial number of significant misstatements of the law, and I also became concerned that the report included modifications of what appeared to me to be regurgitations of doctrine, military doctrine related to the use of fire support assets, and based on that conclusion, I informed the Gotovina Defence that I did feel that I could and that I should offer my opinion on what I considered to be the flaws or the errors in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us talk about a few items in this report and maybe we can elaborate on your last statement just a bit more. And let us begin, for instance, on the first page under 1(c)(iv). Without reading everything that is above, the statement that Lieutenant-Colonel Konings had was: "The above-stated purpose of the support -- of fire support leads to the preliminary conclusion that fire support should not be used against civilian targets." Now was that particular comment significant to you when you read it, Professor, and why?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: It was significant to me, and it really jumped out at me right at the beginning for a number of reasons. First off, I am more than familiar with the style of US Army doctrinal writing. It was apparent to me that, reading up to that point, what I was reading was a copy of US Army military doctrine and I didn't pull the fire support doctrine to validate that. It was kind of an instinctual reaction. But that number 4 was inconsistent with the rest of the provision, so it looked to me like it was an addition to what had otherwise been a statement of military doctrine, and it was somewhat internally contradictory. As an expert on the Law of Armed Conflict my reaction was there is no such thing as a civilian target. A target is lawful military objective. A civilian is presumptively immune from being made the object of attack, unless and until the civilian takes a direct part in hostilities at which point they cease to benefit from their civilian immunity. So the terminology that fire support will not be used against civilian targets is -- it's axiomatic, that the notion that you will make a civilian a target is a -- it wouldn't be -- you wouldn't use that terminology in military doctrine. You would say fire support should never be used to target immune people or places, or civilians are immune from being made the object of attack, not conflating the words "civilian" and "target."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn the page in English, and I would like to show you another portion and that is in the paragraph towards the bottom of the page where you see H.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you scroll down just a little bit there. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you would not mind that I'm trying to seek clarification of the previous answer of the witness. You're mainly concerned about the language used. You do not disagree in any way, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly do not disagree with the proposition that civilians are immune from being made the object of attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore should never be targeted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should not be targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was concerned that the terminology reflected both a supplement to the doctrinal provision that -- that it was connected to and also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what way a supplement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In other words, up to that point, I'm reading what is operational doctrine. That Roman numeral IV is an addition of -- it's an effort to supplement that with a rule from the Law of Armed Conflict, but it is inartfully phrased which suggests to me that it was not written by a Judge Advocate General who was involved in the doctrinal development or review process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You explained to us that you would never use the word "civilian target" because civilians are immune from -- at least should be. It is self-exploratory; you don't have to tell it. Could the difference be that the language used by Mr. Konings allows for the possibility that someone is illegally targeting civilians and that he expresses that. Whereas you say, Don't use that language because you would never fire at a target which -- of the kind Mr. Konings considers to be civilian; that is because of its civilian character immune from attack not being a military target which could be attacked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That it was my absolute conclusion. That's exactly what I felt. I -- I had no problem understanding the import of what was said. It was an indication to me, though, my first indication as I'm reading this that something had been added to the doctrinal discussion that led up to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what now exactly was added?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That provision that was an obvious effort to articulate a basic rule of the Law of Armed Conflict, that because civilians are immune from being made the object of attack they should not -- shall never be made the object of the use of indirect fire. But the terminology caught my attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but there's nothing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The word choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there's nothing in the substance --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with which you would disagree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us move on to the next page that we were about to address, and that is in paragraph 8. Excuse me, H. The -- should be on page 2 and it says: "The fire support system is a system that supports and enables military operations and should therefore only be used for targeting military targets. Only in a case of self-defence military -- only in a case of self-defence military units (including fire support units) may be forced to fire on civilian targets." Can you comment on that inclusion in Lieutenant-Colonel Konings's report?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yes, that's another provision that immediately caught my attention, again because, while I think I understood the essence of what was being said, the -- the way it was expressed I thought was dangerously overbroad. The suggestion, I think, or the intent was to suggest that civilians are immune from being made the object of attack, unless and until they trigger a right to act in self-defence because they've taken a direct part in hostilities. But the way it's phrased is far more overbroad than that. It would suggest that any time a military commander felt that targeting an immune civilian would contribute to the defence of his or her forces, then would it would be justified. And that's improper. And so, again, it looked to me like an area that -- or a provision that was included in another -- in an otherwise broad adoption of a doctrinal statement, but the way it was phrased suggested to me it was not written by somebody with expertise in the Law of Armed Conflict because of its overbreadth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was going to proceed in this vein. I don't know if you want to take a break at this point, or have me proceed. I will gladly do either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's the right time to have a break. Mr. Corn, we will have a break. We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, if we could move to page 5 of Lieutenant-Colonel Konings's report, and I'd like to address a couple of other items. And on that first carry-over paragraph, Professor, before the (b), I would just like to focus you on the sentence of: "Artillery assets can only" -- Do you see that see, sir? "Artillery assets can only be used," do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the carry-over paragraph, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: On page 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On page 5 of the report. Do you see paragraph (b), sir?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Right above paragraph (b).

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it's the sentence that begins: "Artillery assets can only be used in -- in case ..."

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm not seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is before paragraph 5 on this page, so apparently paragraph 4, last line before subparagraph (b).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay I see it, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. That sentence written by Lieutenant-Colonel Konings: "Artillery assets can only be used in case of the safe distance between the expected impacts and the civilian population is big enough to avoid casualties." Can you give us your assessment of that comment by Colonel Konings?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Well, once again I think I understood the general idea that he was trying to convey, but it was an imprecise and potentially dangerous imprecise articulation of the rule. What he essentially is saying is that you are only permitted to use artillery assets when you know that they will not cause civilian casualties. If that were it the rule in the Law on Armed Conflict we wouldn't have a proportionality rule. Because a proportionality rule is in effect an acknowledgement in the law that commanders conducting operations will inevitably have to make a judgement as to whether an attack that they know is probably going to cause civilian casualties may or may not be conducted. And that judgement is based on the assessment of the anticipated collateral damage or incidental injury and a comparison of that damage to the anticipated military advantage, and a determination as to whether or not that anticipated civilian harm will be excessive. This is a misstatement of the law, because what it says is, you cannot use artillery unless you know that it won't cause civilian casualties. If that -- again, if that were the law we wouldn't need the proportionality rule. So it jumped out at me as not only an addition to the doctrinal statement that it was connected to, but an addition that suggested a rule that was more restrictive than the law actually establishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with the -- that page, Professor, I'd like to move down to the first several sentences in paragraph (b): "Targeting of pure civilian targets will be out of the question, since an operation at the tactical level is planned and executed against military targets. Military targets" -- excuse me. "Military targets inside civilian-populated areas will only be attacked according to the rules of engagement and collateral damage estimates set by the highest tactical commander or in some cases even by the operational or strategic commander." And there are a lot of concepts in there that talk about rules of engagement and collateral damage, but could you give us your assessment of that comment by Colonel Konings?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Well, first off, the first sentence is under-inclusive. It says: "Targeting of pure civilian targets will be out of the question, since an operation at the tactical level is planned and executed against military targets." Operations at the tactical, operational and strategic level may only be planned against military objectives. So -- I mean, it's accurate in the sense that tactically you're only allowed to engage military objectives but it's under-inclusive but it seems to limit the rule to the tactical context. But what really struck me about that paragraph was I started to realise at that point that this author was conflating the restrictions of rules of engagement with the Law of Armed Conflict. I obviously knew this report was written by a career officer from the Netherlands. I know from my experience that the Dutch Army has extensive experience dealing with NATO rules of engagement. I was really unsurprised at this point that this condition flakes was occurring because this is a very common mistake that operators make. They're used to operating within the constraints established by rules of engagement. Rules of engagement are a tactical and operational control measure imposed by national or multi-national authorities to manage the battle space and the application of combat power, and make sure that that application is consistent with political objectives, policy objectives and the Law of Armed Conflict. Rules of engagement must be consistent with the Law of Armed Conflict but they are not synonymous with the Law on Armed Conflict. In many instances they are more restrictive than the Law of Armed Conflict. And when I read that paragraph, it illuminated for me what was going on in this report. This was an officer that was assuming that the experience he had had operating under restrictive rules of engagement was, in fact, the law that operated to define what was or what was not the permissible application of combat power in an armed conflict, and it produces a mischaracterisation of the law. For example, in that paragraph, in the second sentence, he tells us that: "Military targets inside civilian populated areas will only be attacked according to the rules of engagement and collateral damage estimates set by higher-level command." If you're operating in an operation for NATO, or for the United States, or for the United Kingdom, that has an extensive process of issuing rules of engagement, that may indeed be true, but that is not because it is required by the Law of Armed Conflict. So if you are not operating under that operational paradigm, then that is not an accurate statement. The ultimate obligation of a commander is to make sure that the engagement of military targets in a populated area is consistent with the Law of Armed Conflict. If that commander's superior authorities impose additional restraints on the execution of operations, whether they call it rules of engagement, operational orders, tactical control measures, or this is what you're allowed to do, then, as a matter of command obligation, that commander has to further restrict his application of combat power, but that's not because the law of war mandates it, or the Law of Armed Conflict. So that revealed to me what I concluded was a systematic flaw in this report, this conflation of two disparate sources of constraint and obligation under the law that -- and policy that regulates contemporary military operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could -- would you allow me to seek some clarification. You say he is wrong here because he is not reflecting Law of Armed Conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. My point is that it's overbroad because it suggests that the rules of engagement are the definitive source of obligation for a military commander. That's true if they exist, if they have been issued, but they cannot modify the obligations of the Law of War by granting additional authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But at least that's how I understood it, your testimony, you say, He's defining matters in a broader sense which goes beyond the limits of what the Law of Armed Conflict allows you to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, my question to you would be: Where do you read that paragraph 4 sets out the limits formulated by the Law of Armed Conflict? Because if I look at it, apparently he's invited, Please explain the considerations that go into targeting, including the levels at which targeting decisions are made, particularly with respect to targets in civilian-populated areas. Where do I find that he is setting out the Law of Armed Conflict, or is he just explaining what, according to him, would be appropriate to do irrespective of what dictated him to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the paragraph is titled -- he is asked to explain considerations that go into the targeting process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then, yes, Your Honour, I agree with you, what he does is he lists doctrinal statement of that targeting cycle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The intelligence preparation of the battlefield leads to the selection and identification of targets and then other factors go into the process. Then he lists operational constraints on the application of combat power but he focuses exclusively on RoE. And I'm not -- I don't want to suggest that, as I say, if RoE is a factor in that process, it is critical factor. I understand that. What it revealed to me was that it seem to be suggesting an assumption that the predominant source of constraint in this targeting process is RoE, and as I say, that's accurate for a country or command that is operating under restrictive RoE, but not necessarily for every armed force or every commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, well, I do not see -- apparently in paragraph 4 he sets out what should be done without putting it clearly in a context of whether this is Law of Armed Conflict --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or not. I do understand that you say if you would focus on Law of Armed Conflict, this would be incorrect, because it goes beyond what is required by the Laws of Armed Conflicts. It is rather rules of engagement. But there is no claim, or at least could you say that it's imprecise, not giving the proper and precise context of these conclusions. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- i think within a little bit broader context it lead to the follow-on of the paragraph. The basic rule will always be not to inflict casualties or damage to civilians or their property. Your Honour, with all due respect, I do not believe that's the basic rule of the Law of Armed Conflict. The basic rule of the Law of Armed Conflict is to always distinguish between lawful military objectives and civilians and civilian property. The proportionality rule establishes the balance that a commander must engage in when he knows an attack on a lawful military objective will produce civilian casualties, collateral damage or incidental injury. So it seemed to me that he -- he takes that rule of engagement and -- and it becomes the basic rule and as -- we know that Additional Protocol I uses that same terminology, the basic rule. The basic rule to distinguish between lawful military objectives and civilians and civilian property. So it's -- in that one specific paragraph or subparagraph, I -- I certainly understand the point that you're raising, that he does not explicitly purport to be defining the Law of Armed Conflict. What it suggested to me was a broader confusion between the constraints that are imposed by policy dictates of commands and the limits on permissible conduct pursuant to the Law of Armed Conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You interpret where he said basic rule is a rule of law rather than a rule of any other kind. That's how you interpret his text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, within the -- within the broader context of the report, my understanding is he's writing this report to define the legal obligations or to eliminate the permissible use of authority to use artillery during the conduct of a military operation related to this trial, so when he uses the term "the basic rule" there, did I automatically say, He's trying to tell us that's the Law of Armed Conflict? No. What I understood that to mean is he is suggesting to us that it is basic principle in the execution of any military operation, including this one, that he's been asked to critique.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, with this conflating of these two rules can you just, before we move off this particular area, just synopsise what problems come to bear when you conflate these two and make statements like, as we saw previously, artillery assets can only be used in case the safe distance between the expected impacts and the civilian population is big enough to avoid casualties.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: This is a -- what I would consider a routine issue when you serve -- in my experience serving as a legal advisor in the US Army. Our commanders and staff officers are so inundated with the rule of engagement process that they start to -- they're essentially taught by implication that rules of engagement are the definitive source of authority and obligation for the conduct of military operations. The danger with that is that rules of engagement are policy restrictions that can be removed just as quickly as they can be established. What they can't do is they can't authorise a scope of authority that exceeds the limits of the Law of Armed Conflict. But they certainly can authorise a scope of authority that's co-extensive with the Law of Armed Conflict. For example, you had rules of engagement during Operation Just Cause in Panama where there was really one rule of engagement: The Panamanian Defence Force has been declared hostile. That meant that military commanders could employ combat power pursuant to the full scope of authority granted under the Law of Armed Conflict. And what this -- the danger here is that it suggests that routine restrictions on that full scope of authority have taken the form of permanent restrictions. And therefore, I've had the personal experience of dealing with commanders in -- in -- in training events where I would give advice that the use of a certain method or means of warfare is legally permissible, and I would get -- the response would be, Well, we -- we're normally allowed to do that under the RoE so that cannot be right. And you had to go through the process of kind of reorienting them to understand that the RoE is a circle of constraint within a broader circle of authority called the Law of Armed Conflict, and it can be modified by whatever authority imposes it. And in fact, a NATO RoE, US RoE, routinely have provisions, even in the most restrictive scenarios. For example, a very common provision, no unobserved indirect fires in populated areas. But in most cases there is a qualifier that that rule is waived under certain tactical situations, when you're in contact, when it's necessary to suppress enemy indirect fire, and that's tactically logical because you will identify an enemy asset that is firing on you through counter-battery radar. Now that's not observed fires because you don't know what is around that artillery asset, but you know exactly where the rounds are coming from. And so there a waiver because there is a tactical or operational necessity that is anticipated that justifies restoring the authority to the full scope permissible under the Law of Armed Conflict. And so the danger with this conflation, and I think it was manifested in this report, is that policy-based constraints take on the character of legal constraints. And I understood this report as a statement of -- from an artillery expert on the permissible use of artillery in populated areas, and it starts to use RoE constraints to suggest that it's not permissible to use artillery per se when there's not a safe distance to ensure an absence of collateral damage and incidental injury. That's overbroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite you again to slow down --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for the interpreters and transcribers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If can you scroll down to the bottom of page 5 going into point 6, and there are several considerations mentioned by Lieutenant-Colonel Konings. And if we can turn to the next page, I would like to direct your attention to a portion of his report at the top of the page and focussing on the two (ii) provision on the top of page 6. Are you with me, Professor?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Once these and other aspects have been considered, the best available asset for the attack will be designated. As accuracy of the attack in order to minimise the risk of collateral damage will be a very crucial aspect, artillery and especially rockets and mortars will be low on the list. Only in case the target is beyond the distance within which collateral damage can occur, the choice to use artillery can be made. This distance is variable and depends on many factors, such as weapon, projectile, weather conditions, position and distance." Now focussing on that particular paragraph, Professor, can you give us the assessment of those comments -- your assessment of those comments by Colonel Konings?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Well, I think it starts off perfectly: "Once these and other aspects have been considered the best available asset for the attack will be designated." That's what we call in the process weaponeering, determining which weapon is best suited under all the circumstances to achieve the desired effect: "As accuracy of the attack, in order to minimise the risk of collateral damage, will be very crucial ... artillery and especially rockets ... will be low on the list." Well, the first prong of that sentence is accurate. That's what military lawyers do in the targeting process. They critique whether or not the weaponeers have selected an asset that comports with the commander's obligation to minimise the risk of collateral damage and incidental injury, and that part again implicates the proportionality analysis. But then the statement rockets and mortars will be low on the list, I think is more of a tactic technique and procedure than doctrine. What weapons system will be low or high on the list is going to be dictated primarily by two considerations: Desired effect and the risk of collateral damage and incidental injury. There may be situations where the nature of the target and the desired effect, and the resources available to the commander, and the enemy situation, and the civilian situation, might produce a conclusion that a use of one of these assets would be higher on the list than -- than cannon artillery or close-air support or -- or -- or rotary-ring aviation or helicopter assets. There is no per se rule, what system is better than another. That is a dangerous proposition because it's that case by case contextual analysis that enables a commander to package the application of combat power in a manner that comport with the fundamental balance that the law seeks to strike between necessity and humanity. He goes on in that paragraph to say: "Only in case the target is beyond the distance within which collateral damage can occur, the choice to use artillery can be made." That sentence directly contradicts the first sentence of that one paragraph. The first sentence says, that you -- I'm sorry, the second sentence. The second sentence says that you have to consider collateral damage as an element in the targeting process. The follow-on sentence creates per se prohibition on collateral damage. If the -- if the follow-on sentence were accurate, then you wouldn't have to consider collateral damage, because would you never be allowed to use a weapon that produced collateral damage. And we know that that's what the Law of Armed Conflict requires. So it's a mix of legitimate considerations and accurate considerations for an artillery expert or an artillery staff officer. I have to consider the weapon, the effect, the enemy, the desired effect for the -- to achieve the commander's intent, the potential collateral damage. But, again, because I think that the instinct to assume that restrictive RoE are in fact the definitive statement of the law has influenced this analysis, it produces these incongruities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last comment on this page, if we turn to 3(i), talking about the effect. Do you see that, sir? "The effect required is also important."

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Artillery is not the weapon system to destroy ... buildings ... capability as a non-lethal weapon system, influencing the" -- and it says "moral" but I believe morale, "component of any opponent." You talk a little bit about this weapon system and the destruction of buildings. Do you have a comment on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yes. So we have to start on page 5 and the question that's posed, subparagraph 6: "Please explain the considerations and constraints that go into determining whether and how to use artillery fire in civilian-populated areas." In subparagraph 3 -- three (iii), the author makes the definitive statement that: "Artillery is not the weapon system to destroy strong buildings." Well, what jumped out at me there was at the very beginning of his report, when he's explaining artillery doctrine, he acknowledges that the fire support system, artillery, is used for many effects other than destruction; harassment, interdiction, neutralisation. It is extremely common for a commander to employ artillery with full knowledge that destruction is not going to be the effect that is going to be achieved because that is not what he needs to achieve. And artillery may, in fact, be an ideal weapons system to produce other affects. So I thought that that was somewhat under-inclusive, because it didn't fully articulate the consideration of use of artillery in a populated area when the effect desired was something other than destruction. And even on the statement itself, I think most experts in military operations would concede that artillery might not always achieve a destructive effect of a building, but what the case by case situational analysis leads to is the requirement of the commander to assess the capability available and the effect he needs to achieve, and select the capability that's most likely to produce that effect. If I'm in a light infantry unit and my heaviest weapons system is cannon artillery, and I believe I have to try and destroy a building, that may in fact be the best capability I have to attempt to achieve that effect. It -- it just depends, as so much of this analysis does. So, again, then the follow-on sentence, to me, jumped out at me because he skips over the other legitimate doctrinal purposes of employment of artillery and seizes on an assertion of what he suggests is an improper purpose, the use of artillery to influence civilian morale. And I don't dispute that. That is an improper purpose of artillery. But what it seemed to me to suggest was that because you can't destroy a target with artillery in a city, then the only other reason you might use it, the only other rational inference is that its use was for the illicit purpose of damaging civilian morale. And by omitting harass, interdict, neutralize, these classic disruption missions, he skips an entire range of possibilities that produce alternate rational inferences other than the two extreme that he offers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We touched on the subject of forward observers, and Colonel Konings talks about this on page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could move ahead to page 8 of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we are talking about the use and significance of forward observers and the appropriate use of them. And if we can turn to paragraph (f) in -- excuse me, subparagraph (f) in paragraph 8. Do you see that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm interested in this paragraph -- at least these sentences of the paragraph: "The use of artillery and mortars against targets in civilian areas without having these targets under observation of a forward observer should not be done, unless the target is beyond the already described collateral damage distance and the exact location is known. But also in this case the commander will want and will need to know the effects of the attack." Can you give us your assessment of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yeah. Again, we start with the question: "Please explain the use and significance of forward observers, including whether it is appropriate to use artillery without forward observers against targets in ... populated areas." So the question seems to invite an assessment of what is legally permissible through the use appropriate [sic]. Now I guess you could say appropriate doesn't necessarily infer that, but it seems to me to certainly suggest that. There is absolutely no dispute that the use of a forward observer for the employment of indirect fires is an ideal situation. It's ideal from an operational standpoint and from a humanitarian standpoint. Operationally it enhances the probability of achieving the desired effect with minimum resources; from a humanitarian standpoint, it gives the commander a better picture of the potential collateral damage and incidental injury. So the suggestion that commanders should always endeavour to place targets under observation or it's ideal would be thorough accurate. The word he uses there is "should." Now "should" is not "must," and I understood that. "Must" would have been more problematic. But again, the tone of that paragraph suggests to me that what the author is -- is saying is that unless you can place targets in a populated area under human observation, you should not target them. I used the example before of counter-battery fire. You just have to imagine one hypothetical. A commander is conducting an operation. Just like his assessment, he knows the enemy will have his command post as one of the highest-value targets on his target list. Now let's imagine his command post starts to come under indirect fire, disrupting the operation, placing the success of his own operation in serious jeopardy. Neutralising the source of that enemy fire is a critical mission. That commander may have counter-battery radar. That radar can precisely identify the source of the enemy artillery to an eight-digit grid coordinate, and it's linked directly to his fire support coordination centre. Literally within seconds, the determination of the source of that artillery can produce a fire mission with his own indirect fire assets, to neutralise that threat. Now, obviously that commander, in that hypothetical, does not have forward observers. He doesn't know if the enemy has located its artillery in a school-yard, in a hospital compound, in a civilian-populated area. He can't know that. But he has to make a tactical judgement as to whether the risk of firing blind is offset by the value of protecting his critical command, control and communications function. In most cases I think a military commander would authorise that counter-batter mission. If you asked the commander, Would you prefer to have eyes on target? Every commander will say, Of course, but it is not an absolutely requirement. It is not a per se prohibition to employ indirect unobserved fires in a populated area. It is, however, a routine constraint in NATO and Western rules of engagement, subject to situational qualifiers that I mentioned before. So for me that explained you shouldn't do this. Because I'm sure that this author's experience was, We will refrain from doing this unless it is absolutely necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let me try to fully understand the testimony of the witness and the paragraph. Apparently in this paragraph, in the beginning, it says you shouldn't -- that shouldn't be done. And then unless, and then part of what you described for us is included in what apparently the author considers to be an exception. That is, the exact location is known as one of the criteria. Whereas, you explained to us that if you have this radar system that more or less is an expression of the same, that you have technical means by which you could very precisely identify the target and you're telling us you might not know whether it's a hospital or not. If you would know the area, would you take that into consideration when finally deciding whether or not you would use that weapons system for that target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- so to that extent it seems that, although in different wordings, that Mr. Konings, You shouldn't do it is conditional as well, just as you explained that there may be many circumstances which would allow for such an action.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the one portion of that sentence, I think, that exposes a significant divergence between his view and mine is he leads into that by saying: "... unless the target is beyond the already described collateral damage distance and its location is precisely known." That suggests to me that what is he saying is, you can fire blind so long as you know that there are no civilians in the area because it would be -- or you're using a weapon that will have an effect that will be confined to an area in that populated environment that cannot affect civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the context of the report, you'll find the language sometimes to be the anticipated risk of collateral damage, which is not a total exclusion of collateral damage. You said if what he says is right, you wouldn't need any rule of proportionality anymore, whereas in the report, he accepts that a rule of proportionality does exist. So to that extent, I'm asking myself where actually you take a substantial different position and where you're unhappy with perhaps sometimes the inconsistency mentioning this and then explaining it a little bit later in a different way. So I'm just trying to find out for myself where actually there is a -- a substantial difference in view on what is permitted and not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my reaction to this, obviously is based on my understanding of what it -- what it purports to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding, as I read it, was, when he used the qualifier "is beyond the already established collateral damage" -- "the already described collateral damage distance," that meant to me that he was saying, You can fire blind so long as you know beforehand that will not produce collateral damage. If that's what it means then I have a substantive disagreement with it. If it means something more tempered, in other words, that if you're going to fire blind you should consider the general location where you've identified the target as part of your proportionality analysis, then I would have no disagreement with it, because I think that is a thoroughly accurate, totally accurate statement of the law. But in the broader context of this paragraph, as the concluding portion of it, the suggestion to me was, unless you have forward observers, unmanned aerial vehicle, video, or some other asset that can you give you full situational awareness, you should not fire unobserved indirect fires. And I think that is a good principle but it is not a -- a per se rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this context could I ask you, the expression used by Mr. Konings, the CDEs, the Collateral Damage Estimates, that is apparently a technical term. I'm not very much familiar with ... First of all, you are familiar with CDEs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the estimate of where no collateral damage could be caused anymore; or is it what is still acceptable as a risk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think -- well, let me -- let me try and answer the CDE question first and then put it in the context of this paragraph if I may. A collateral damage estimate is produced in a very mature targeting process for pre-planned targets. So, for example, you identify potential targets, and then the experts on the effects of weapons and the civil affairs experts, who can kind of give their best estimate of what civilians are in that area, work together to estimate that if we used this weapons system what is the probability that there will be collateral damage or incidental injury, and what is the scope of that collateral damage or incidental injury, so that when it comes time to execute that mission the commander has a pre-established assessment that can he use to inform him in his proportionality analysis. So it is an estimate of risk. What he says in this paragraph is unless the target is beyond the already described collateral damage distance, in other words, that you've pin-pointed the target but because of your pre-existing assessment, you can say with a certain degree of certainty that targeting that target with this weapons system will not produce collateral damage, then you can use it blind. And that's certainly true. I mean, that would be ideal. Right? If can I take out that enemy artillery with a high degree of confidence that I will not produce collateral damage, that's an ideal scenario. What I don't think he accounts for is the risk that the use of the system will not be beyond the pre-determined collateral damage estimate, and yet you still have a pin-point location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You very much therefore interpret, then, the language of Mr. Konings to be that when he talks about in accordance with collateral damage estimates that that he aims at excluding or an almost zero probability of collateral damage instead of a risk of collateral damage which is in accordance with generally accepted rules.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And that's mainly because of the word "distance" instead of "estimate." But if the understanding is he means it is a factor in the proportionality analysis, I thoroughly agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last comment on this report that I would like to bring to your attention would be at page 13, paragraph 12. And maybe we can look at these paragraphs 12 and 13 together. But in paragraph 12, the question for Colonel Konings is: "Please explain the use and/or constraints in using the weapons ... in question 9 against targets in civilian-populated areas." And weapons, number 9, uses a variety of weaponry. I'd like to focus towards the end of that paragraph: "The relative inaccuracy and high number of projectiles needed ..." Do you see?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "... form a high risk towards civilians in the same area, it is the balance between the importance of the target, the enormous negative effect of causing casualties to the civilian population, the risk of their own forces, and the availability of alternatives that will bring a commander to decide to use artillery or not. And practically 100 per cent one will decide not to use artillery." If we go down to the last sentence in paragraph 13: "Therefore, uncorrected fire should not be used in civilian-populated areas." Tell us your commentary on those two provisions, Professor.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Let's start with the last sentence of paragraph 13. It relates back to the dialogue that I just had with the Court. And I think it is a fairly categorical statement that the meaning of that prior paragraph we discussed was unobserved indirect fires may not be used in populated areas. "Uncorrected" is a synonym for "unobserved." Correcting fire is the product of having an observer adjust fire from the point of that indirect shot. So uncorrected means it's firing without direct observation. As for the prior paragraph, and what we are talking about here are a variety of cannon and rocket artillery assets. And that last sentence is -- I mean, I just have to say it is incredibly overbroad. In practicality, 100 per cent of the time a commander will decide not to use artillery in a populated area. In fact, the history of even contemporary military operations totally rebuts that assumption. My own experience, my first real experience with the realities of combat, and I wasn't there at the time but I had recently left Panama and my unit was involved so I was very -- obviously very concerned what was going on. In Operation Just Cause, in 1989, one of the highest value targets was the Panamanian Defence Force Comandancia, their headquarters building. That Comandancia couldn't have been located in a worse position for purposes of collateral damage. It was in the heart of a neighbourhood called Chorillo [phoen], which was an impoverished area of Panama City that was basically a community of ramshackle wooden structures, and that Comandancia was put under intense indirect fire at the very outset of the mission, resulted in substantial civilian casualties, which were very unfortunate. I think the commander must have known that there was a high probability of producing civilian casualties. We can fast-forward to the first Gulf war, the use of indirect fires against populated areas in both the air and ground phase of that operation. A cruise missile is indirect fire. And there were literally hundreds of cruise missiles fired against military objectives in the city of Baghdad during that mission. The air war against Serbia; another example. The operation in -- against Iraq in 2003. There were -- the enemy used populated areas as strongholds and allied forces routinely used indirect fires to facilitate the defeat of these enemy forces. What is essential is that a commander contemplating the employment of that compatibility be aware of the obligations under the law and factor in the risk of collateral damage and incidental injury into the equation of whether that asset should be used. But there are many -- we could literally spend hours going over hypotheticals where a commander with an arsenal of capabilities would make a determination that indirect fire was the best capability to achieve a certain effect in a populated area. And that's an unfortunate reality of warfare. But to suggest that because indirect fire cannot achieve a destructive effect and the targets in a populated area oftentimes are structures that can't be destroyed easily with indirect fire you're never going to use indirect fire in that area, I think is -- is a distortion of both doctrine and the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could I seek clarification. How do you read the line: "In practically 100 per cent one will not decide to use artillery." Would that mean in close to 100 per cent or effectively you would never use that? What's -- how do you understand the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood it as effectively you would never use this asset in a populated area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I -- I'm a native-speaking person of the same language as Mr. Konings is. It sounds to me very much practically here a translation of a Dutch word "praktisch" which would mean "close to." Your comments were based on your understanding. Could you give your comments as well on the understanding of this line, to say that in close to 100 per cent, almost 100 per cent, one will decide not to use artillery.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's equally overbroad, Your Honour. I think that it is a -- and that's not from a legal perspective. That's from an operational perspective. I think if you go back and review the very doctrine that's been included in this report, as you note -- noted in your discussion with me earlier, even the author acknowledges that collateral damage assessments and proportionality are routine elements in the assessment of the use of indirect fires in populated areas. The doctrine itself reveals to us that there's expectation that commanders are going to have to make these assessments and employ this asset for certain effects. This is a routine aspect of military operations. So even if we qualify it and say, Not 100 per cent of the time, but almost never, I think is overbroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you that your comment and your main criticism of the report is that where it may contain all the relevant elements for decision making, that at the end we always find sweeping statements which you say are not justified by what the author said before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's one of my criticisms of the report, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can just follow up on Judge Orie's statement. That's one of your criticisms. Can you synopsise, before we move off this document, the balance of your criticisms concerning this report with -- taking into consideration what you talked about the conflation of rules of engagement and Laws of Armed Conflict?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
