utterances.text: I think the first point is that I -- I believe that many of the rules of a constraint that were included in the report were not derived from the doctrine that was generally reproduced in the report. It was an addition to the doctrine, which, theoretically is -- I have no objection to. I mean, that's -- you're an expert and you're rendering a report and if you think that you -- it is appropriate or beneficial to the finder of fact to add or modify doctrine, great. But then what troubled me was the doctrine or the language that was added, in my view, was not an accurate statement of the law that it purported or the constraints that it purported to articulate. That, I think, was produced primarily from this systemic conflation of rules of engagement and the Law of Armed Conflict. So I -- I have -- as a matter of fact, I'm sympathetic to it because I have experienced this with operators I have dealt with all through my career. I understand -- I think I understand what happened. What troubled me more than that, however, was the modifications to the doctrine itself, like the last portion of the report we just discussed, Your Honour, where you take a series of legitimate doctrinal considerations for the employment of indirect fire in a populated area, and you produce a conclusion that I think is inconsistent with the practice of military operations that inform the doctrine, and that to me was more troubling. Now, I don't purport to be -- I have never been an artillery officer. I haven't attended artillery courses, and I don't purport have the expertise on artillery that Colonel Konings has. I'm sure he knows about artillery. But at -- I can't help but look at this as a lawyer, because that's what I am, and what I saw was a distortion of the rules of constraint that was explicable but a distortion of doctrine that was less explicable, and that's what I tried to point out to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, I would like to shift back and just make some final clarifications on some acronyms, if I can, in Professor Corn's report and then I will be completed. So if we can go back to D1642, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can go back to this report. As we note that the date on the bottom of this report, Mr. President, is -- actually was provided on June the 22nd, and that would have to be corrected on -- in paragraph 10. Our records reflect it was sent on -- not on July 22nd, as you see in paragraph 10 of the supplemental information sheet, D1643. So we would like to correct that erroneous -- if you see paragraph 10 says July, Professor Corn provided that in June 22nd. Mr. President, it's from the proof -- in the supplemental information sheet, paragraph 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But for Mr. Corn to be informed that the first Monday of the month, there's a testing system of our sirens for other circumstances. That's what you hear at this moment, Mr. Corn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I noticed an error in the English transcript. May I point that out because I think it is an important point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, although it will be reviewed overnight anyhow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but please -- no, but, please, it could that be it would be overlooked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 20 -- on line 21, 12:01:07, the word "explicable" should have been "inexplicable."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that is page 59, line 20 -- excuse me, 21, excuse me. That was explicable but a distortion of doctrine that was inexplicable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I remember Mr. Corn told us. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I can just take a few minutes just to clarify some of these acronyms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 23 in your report, Professor. And about midway through that first paragraph you are talking about -- before you start talking about these military objectives you use this line, middle of that paragraph: "General Gotovina's intelligence indicated that in addition to being a C3I centre for enemy forces, there were other aspects of the enemy disposition within Knin." I'm focusing on the C3I and what that means?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: It's an acronym for command, control, communication, and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying on that page, and if we just focus on the paragraph B with the 7th Krajina Corps headquarters, would your opinion concerning this target change whether the commander of the 7th Krajina Corps was present in that headquarters or not?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move to page 27 and the first full paragraph on page 27. This is the section of your report where you talked about Falkland Islands campaign, and I'm looking at the first full paragraph, Professor, and I believe it is -- begins four lines down: "Even if his assets were insufficient ..." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Even if his assets were insufficient to destroy targets in Knin, creating the perception of 'full spectrum operational dominance' would be beneficial to degrade the ability of the enemy to respond to his attack." I'm interested in this comment of full spectrum operational dominance, and essentially what is that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: The notion of full spectrum operational dominance is convincing your opponent that you possess the initiative at every phase of that military operation, every aspect; the close fight, the deep fight, the future fight. Sometimes you will see this referred to attacking in operational depth, all right. So what I'm discussing here is that -- particularly during a deliberate attack of prepared defensive positions, a commander wants to convey to the enemy that he possesses the initiative at every phase of the fight and that the enemy -- and he wants to dictate the terms of the battle to the enemy. He wants to control the tempo of the battle, and that requires him to demonstrate to the enemy his ability to effect the outcome of the battle in operational depth, across the full spectrum of the operation, so that the enemy thinks that all aspects of this fight are dominated by the opponent. The greater the ability to demonstrate full spectrum dominance the greater the probability that your enemy will capitulate rapidly, because the enemy will see the futility in trying to match your attack at any level or at any phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn to page 28. Again, this is another clarification, Professor. In the centre of that page, the paragraph beginning: "Based on these facts ..." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Based on these facts, General Gotovina could have reasonably assumed that the substantially reduced civilian population of Knin would have 'gone to ground' and would generally not be exposed to the effects of indirect fire [sic] during curfew hours." This concept that you put in there, "gone to ground," what are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: It is a colloquialism for seeking shelter, finding the best place to be out of harm's way. It's a common term in the US military vernacular, The enemy or the civilians have gone to ground. They're out of -- they've gotten as much safety as they can find.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And understand these circumstances did you conclude that that was reasonable assumption by General Gotovina of these individuals going to ground?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: As I say in the report, I think that would have been a reasonable assumption. I think if I had been in the targeting cell during the planning for this mission, under those facts and assumptions, I think I would have had the same assumption, that this is a time of day, under the circumstances, where there's a high probability that the civilians will have done their best to be out of harm's way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My last clarification is on page 31 of your report, sir. As it's the paragraph beginning: "The timing of employment ..." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I'm interested in your comment five lines -- excuse me, four lines down, where you note: "Surging fires against C3I logistics and reinforcement targets at this point would contribute to the sense of confusion and isolation among defending forces." I'm interested in the clarification on the concept of what you mean by surging fires?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Maximising. Applying the principle of mass. This is written in relation to the overall -- the facts and assumptions that explain to me the overall employment pattern of indirect fires. Based on those facts and assumptions, I concluded that the primary objective of indirect fire was to support the close fight, the tactical execution of the deliberate attack and penetration of enemy defensive positions. Each morning, presumptively when that close fight kicked off, there was a surge of artillery indirect fire assets at command, control and communications facilities in the enemy's rear area in Knin. To me, that is consistent with a logical doctrinal application of that combat power because it is at that decisive point in the tactical fight where you have the greatest need to confuse the enemy, and more importantly, to render the enemy's higher level command and control blind as to what is happening at the close fight, because that contributes to the isolation of the defending forces, their sense that they're out of contact with their support elements, and the probability that it's going to contribute to the capitulation or penetration of those defensive positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My last acronym that you use in several instances through your reports is the concept of METT-T-C, M-E-E-T-T-T-C [sic], can you tell us what that is and can you explain it?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: METT-T-C is a US military acronym that stands Mission, Enemy, Troops, Terrain, Time, and Civilians. It's a shorthand acronym that is used to remind a commander or an operational leader at every level, from a team leader to a corps commander, that operational decisions are always driven by the situational analysis of these factors. And even you can see this throughout Colonel Konings's, he talks about the considerations that go into the target decision-making process. He doesn't uses the term METT-T-C, but if you think about it, it is exactly what he is saying. You look at the resources he has, troops; you look at the mission you have to acquire, effects; you look at the enemy, intelligence; preparation of the battlefield. You look at the terrain. That's part of the IPB process, intelligence preparation of the battlefield. You look at the time. What is the time constraint for achieving this mission or this effect, and you look at the effect on civilian population. METT-T-C. And I use it throughout the report to emphasise that target decision-making processes are inevitably situationally driven, and all of these factors are variable in any given situation. That's why the per se conclusions troubled me, because you can change the weight of each of these factors in any given situation and produce a different outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Corn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would have -- in a similar area I would have -- I'm seeking clarification of one term you're using. You are talking about operational law. Now, I do understand that it's not -- that there is operational and non-operational law, but is my understanding right, that you call operational law that portion of the Law of Armed Conflict which directly deals with operations; or is it -- because you're talking about international law and operational law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was -- it's not a term I'm very familiar with it but I see that you have handbooks on international operational law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know exactly -- I think it was in your CV, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably as a professor of international and operational law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- publications, I see, international and operational law desk book. I saw it ... well, you're using this term a couple of times. It is only one of the sources.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Operational law, Your Honour, would refer to the -- the full body of law that would regulate the planning and execution of military operations. In the context of my report, operational law would mean what you -- as you characterize it, the Law on Armed Conflict that regulates the application of combat power, because that's what I was opining on. If you talk about what is the operational law handbook, the operational handbook is much broader than that because it addresses national legal authorities that influence the planning and execution of military operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that could be to some extent constitutional law, administrative law, all kinds of law --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but the Law of Armed Conflict directly related to operational matters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would be part of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then now I better understand what operational law means. Mr. Russo, I'm looking at the clock. Would it not be better that we first have a break and that you would -- but first let me inquire. There was no -- was there any cross-examination by the other Defence teams. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There will be no questions from us, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, likewise, no questions from us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Yes, that was what was in my memory, so therefore I was addressing you, Mr. Russo. Wouldn't it be better that we would start cross-examination after the break. You would then have another one hour and five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break first, and we will resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Corn -- no, I should say, Professor Corn, because you appear as an expert witness, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Russo. Mr. Russo is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I wanted to begin by asking you a few questions about the information contained in your supplemental information sheet, which has now been marked as Exhibit D1643. If you could turn that to that in your package there; I don't have if you have the page. I want to be sure and maybe you can help me, does this document contain information about every contact you've had with the Gotovina Defence?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I mean, there have been numerous e-mails that have been sent on scheduling issues, and when we were going talk and setting up discussions, but substantively, to the best of my recollection, this is an accurate description of the substantive interactions we've had related to the different products that have been produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So you're comfortable stating that none of the e-mails or other items of correspondence that have been passed between yourself and the Gotovina Defence, none of those contain anything substantive regarding questions you asked them, questions they may have asked you, anything substantive with regard to either your report or your addendum or your anticipated testimony. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that's correct. Because I always knew that there were meetings in the future so I would write an e-mail and say I have some ideas I want to bring up when we meet, but those would have been contained here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, you were originally retained to offer advice on the expert report and addendum of Lieutenant-Colonel Konings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I was originally contacted and asked to -- to consider whether I could do that and possibly be a witness for the Defence, but I was told at that point the initial focus was to give my views on the report and that we weren't -- they weren't sure at that point whether they would need me as a Defence witness or not. We would address that in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: But you did have discussions with them at that point, I believe early December 2008, that there was a possibility that you could testify as a Defence expert; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I was told that they might want to call me as a Defence expert. We didn't discuss the substance of that. The focus then was on this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if I understand your supplemental information sheet correctly, the first time that you delivered to the Gotovina Defence your opinion about the expert report and addendum of Lieutenant-Colonel Konings came in late December of 2008, at a meeting in Tampa, Florida; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Just one second. I -- my recollection is that I had a meeting with one of the counsel in -- my home in Houston before I went to Tampa. So there was a meeting in Tampa -- in Houston, I believe, before I went to Tampa.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at paragraph 2 of your supplemental information sheet, it indicates that shortly after some time-frame in early December 2008, you met with a member of the Defence team --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- at your home in Houston. And it says "to discuss my review of the report and addendum. And then it indicates that at that time you were offered a DVD with a number of documents relating to the use of artillery but you explained that it was not necessary for your analysis at that point to review any documents. So I take it that at that time that you had been offered those documents when counsel came to your home, you hadn't actually conducted your analysis of Lieutenant-Colonel Konings's report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: No, that is incorrect. When I received the report I did my initial review of it. And I notified them that I was ready to talk to them about some concerns I had with the report. The -- the general nature of those concerns is consistent with the discussion that I just engaged in during the direct examination and with the Court. One of the members of the Defence team flew to Houston to meet with me so I could explain to him what I considered to be these errors in the analysis in the report. At that time, he brought this CD but my critique of the report was focussed on the type of systematic flaws that I just explained in the direct examination, and it was after that, when he took my initial critique -- I guess, a summary of my initial critique back to the team that I was invited to meet with the entire team to review the same information with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I just want to be clear: Had you delivered any indication to the Gotovina Defence regarding what your opinions were prior to being offered the DVD with the documents? Even of a general nature.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Before the counsel flew to Houston to meet with me, I had gone through the -- Colonel Konings's report and I had told them that I think there are significant flaws with it that I would like to review with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do you know what documents were on that DVD? Did you ever look at them?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: There were documents that were on that DVD that I believe I was provided in hard copy at a later date. I didn't look at the DVD at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And what makes you believe that the hard copy documents you later looked at were actually on that DVD?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Because my understanding was documents on the DVD were documents from the trial, and other exhibits, and then I was told later that they would send me hard copy versions of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: But in fact you hadn't actually reviewed any documents other than the report and the addendum before you drew your conclusions and offered your opinions about the problems you perceived in the report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And when you say that you reviewed Colonel Konings's report and addendum, there are attachments to both of those. Did you review all of the attachments to both the expert report and the addendum, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: What I recall was that the addendum had assumptions related to different target sets that I did review, as part of the review.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: There was also a list of documents which Lieutenant-Colonel Konings had reviewed, which was submitted along with his addendum. Did you see that list of documents?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: After the meeting you had with counsel at your home, the next meeting you had was the meeting at Tampa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And that meeting is addressed in paragraph 4 in your supplemental information sheet. And you indicate: "At that time, I recall reviewing some of the documents that purportedly were used by Lieutenant-Colonel Konings in preparing his report and addendum." Can tell the Trial Chamber what those documents specifically were?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Specifically I don't recall the title of every document. I think I reviewed a document -- I know I looked at a document of an initial summary of effects of targeting. I looked at the facts and assumptions related to the target sets that he was analysing in the addendum, so it may have been the same information that was embedded within his addendum. The -- I was shown some aerial photographs. The thing that was most significant for me at that point in time was an oral kind of laydown of Operation Storm, kind of an operational summary that was provided and we used photographs, we used some maps. There were -- periodically a counsel would pull out a document that would corroborate something related to the oral explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I want to get to the oral explanation in a minute but I just want to pin down first the documentation that you indicate was purportedly used by Lieutenant-Colonel Konings in preparing his addendum and report. Were any of those documents HV documents?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I know that I looked at operational summaries produced by the HV. I don't know if -- when I talk about the information used by Colonel Konings, my recollection is I was looking at the information, the facts and assumptions embedded in the report that described each target and target set, and effects that occurred on that target. So did I see operational summaries produced by the HV in that meeting? My recollection is probably yes. But I don't know that that was given to me and -- in the context of, This is something that he considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the oral presentation, I'd like you to be as specific as you're able to be and recall for us what information you were provided with during that oral presentation.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: As specific as I can be, I needed -- I felt I needed to get a better sense of the operational situation before I could start giving my own assessment of the propriety of using a certain asset in a certain context. So I was given a -- there was a map on the table, there was another one on the wall and there was a broad-brush explanation of the operational objectives of Operation Storm, the general disposition of friendly and enemy forces leading up to Operation Storm, the relationship -- the strategic relationship between Operation Storm and relief of an area that was -- a Bosnian Muslim area that was besieged at the time. Then there was a discussion of the initiation of the operation. I saw photographs and maps that identified some of the targets that were listed in the addendum within Knin. I wanted to see the dispersion of targets in the city, because I thought that was important. There was explanation of what -- what those some of those assets were. I would probe that to a certain degree, what units were there, what was manufactured there, where did this bridge lead to, where did this rail line lead to. And then was a kind of discussion of the progression of the battle, the first day, the assault, the pincer assault on the Serb -- there was like an intrusion, the Serb lines, the actions of the first night where there was a decision to evacuate civilians from Knin and to tighten the Serb defensive lines, to shorten their defensive lines. The second-day operations. The egress route was in existence for the Serb civilians and military personnel. There was a discussion of the disposition of General Gotovina's artillery assets prior to the battle. The -- there was some visual explanation of the location of those assets and the ability of those assets to put in range of their fires, targets and other area within Knin leading up to the battle. There was discussion of the fact that indirect fire was not used until the assault was commenced. There was discussions ever opportunities that existed to -- to close the egress route by General Gotovina's forces or to target -- potentially target mixed civilian and military personnel that were withdrawing from the pocket, the decision not to do that. And then was some discussion of the concept of the operation for follow-on operations, although I wasn't particularly interested in the next phase of the operation, once Knin had been -- Knin had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You have quite a capacious memory, Professor, and thank you for that level of detail. I want to be clear. This was -- sounds to me as though it was a bit of a back-and-forth discussion. They were informing you about the operational situation. You were asking specific questions, and they were providing answers to those questions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You did mention photographs and documents that you were shown. Do you know whether those photographs and documents are contained within the list of exhibits in paragraph 12 of your supplemental information sheet?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I couldn't say with absolute certainty that every photograph or document is listed there.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: May I continue? I can tell you that -- that I can recall from that meeting which ones I considered to be significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what those were?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: There was a -- there was a battle damage assessment that was conducted -- a report of a battle damage assessment that was provided by a UN observer, I believe. I thought that was significant, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Is that the same document which is addressed, in fact, in the last question of your addendum.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Let me go back and look.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Exhibit P64.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Let me go to the last page. Yes, that's the provisional assessment I'm referring to. And I thought that it was useful to see the location of the military objectives that were within Knin on photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And was this one photograph of -- an aerial photograph of Knin or was it several photographs?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: As I recall, there was more than one aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were there any other documents that stand out in your mind as significant?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Not that I can recall from that meeting, as me leaving with a sense that that was a pretty important piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you take any of these documents with you when you left the meeting?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were any of those documents sent to you prior to the drafting of either your expert report or the addendum?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell me which of those documents you received prior -- and why don't we take this piece by piece, because I understand that the report and addendum were done at different times. Did you receive documentation prior to the drafting of the expert report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I noticed that Mr. Misetic, in his role as slowing down everyone, has now extended his functions to the Prosecution. He is hinting with his hand that you should perhaps slow down, and I agree with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I will pay more attention to Mr. Misetic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat the question, Professor?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: No, I understand the question. As the information sheet indicates, I was given a CD prior to writing my critique of Colonel Konings's expert report. At that point, my critique was focussed on methodology, and I didn't rely on any of that information in that initial report. Prior to writing my addendum, I was sent a -- a number of documents. I went as -- as is indicated in the information sheet, I went back to the Defence team and proposed an alternate methodology. My view was that if I was going to write the addendum which was offering my opinion on the legality of engaging targets with certain weapons systems, I needed to have a sense of the facts and assumptions that were available to General Gotovina that were established by the record, and I felt that it would be much more legitimate for me to have counsel identify those facts and assumptions than for me to go through the record and attempt to discern what information had been well established, what information was contradicted. I haven't been sitting through the trial. So I asked -- may I finish? I asked Defence counsel to give me that information, because the first step in the target assessment process is to gather facts and come up with your assumptions related to the mission. Now what I asked for them to do was to provide facts and assumptions based on their sense of confidence that those facts and assumptions were supported by the record. After they sent them to me, which is in the letter requesting the addendum, I went back to them as I was preparing it, and I asked them very directly if they were confident that these are facts and assumptions that are before the Tribunal. Their response was they were very confident that, based on their assessment of the case, these are legitimate facts and assumptions. They said there are several that they think are more in controversy than others, but that they were comfortable with me framing my opinion or building my opinion on that factual and assumptive foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, although you jumped ahead of me a little bit, I certainly do want to discuss your suggestion of the alternative method. But I was first trying to determine what documents you actually reviewed prior to the drafting of your expert report before discussing what you did with the addendum. Now, if I understand the situation correctly, you had a DVD in hand with documents, at least in late December. You hadn't reviewed those documents before coming to an opinion about Konings's report and addendum. You were then asked to produce your own report addressing some of those issues. Did you, before you drafted the first report, review the documents contained on that DVD?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you review any other documents before you drafted the first report?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Well, it was drafted after the meeting in Tampa, so, as I said, there were documents that I looked at during that meeting in the context of the overall explanation of the operation. But when I sat down to write that report, what I was asked to write was to summarize or explain the legal principles related to the use of indirect fire, in large measure to correct what I saw were overbroad or imprecise assertions of obligation in Colonel Konings's report. So it was more a discussion of relevant law and principles than a discussion of the specific application in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And to be clear, your first report, as you indicate, was an exposition on the state of the Law of Armed Conflict as it relates to the use of artillery in civilian-populated areas and the considerations attendant to that, but I also get the sense that it was in response to the problems you identified in the Konings's report and addendum. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I don't know about addendum. It was primarily focussed on the initial report, and it was responsive because I was -- I was memoralising the oral critique that I had provided of that report to Defence counsel, both at my home and in Tampa during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And is there any particular reason why in your expert report you didn't specifically reference Colonel Konings's report or point out the particular parts that you took issue with, or, for that matter, give any indication that the genesis of your report was a response to Colonel Konings's report?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: No. I mean, I was asked after I had the oral discussions -- I guess that's redundant. After I had the discussions in Tampa with Defence counsel, they followed up based on some of the points I had raised with a letter requesting me to address specific points, okay? When I got that letter, I responded to them and suggested modification of some of them because I thought that some were either redundant or weren't an accurate articulation of the general subject that I had discussed in the meeting. They responded that I could modify it any way I thought made it consistent with my oral discussions, and that was the framework of questions that I responded to in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And attached to your expert report is a May 19th letter, and we've also seen today D1644 which is the March 27th letter. The March 27th letter is the one that lays out the questions for your initial report. Now, did you make modifications to the questions in the March 27 letter or was there earlier correspondence that had different questions which you changed?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: No. I had a phone call, and -- after the meeting in Tampa, and there was a discussion of the points that I had raised from counsel's notes that they thought it would be useful to have a written explanation of. I suggested that they put those points in writing and provide them to me. When I got them, and I started to basically scope out my response to these questions, I felt that it would facilitate my written, or product, to modify some of those questions, so I went back to them and told them I wanted to modify some of the -- the style or the focus of some of the questions, and they said, That was our best recollection of the points you'd made but this is your report, so modify it any way you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm trying to get at is, is the March 27th letter, is that after the modification, or did you modify the questions in the March 27th letter?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I -- I don't know the exact date I wrote the report. My recollection is that I told them after I got the letter I was going to change the form of some of the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So we wouldn't expect to find two letters sent to you with questions in them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Looking at your supplemental information sheet, paragraph 6, you indicate that you provided the Defence with a draft report on or about April 10th, 2009, and that you didn't receive any substantive comments about that report. Were you asked any questions concerning what was contained in that report?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I was not. In fact, I didn't hear anything after I sent it, and, you know, pride of authorship, I'm wondering if -- how it was received. So after waiting a few weeks I contacted them and I said, Are you satisfied with the report? And they said, There are just a couple of typographical errors we noticed and we'll let you -- and we'll send that to you, but, otherwise, we think it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The next paragraph indicates: "During this time-frame, I was provided with a copy of the complete transcript of the trial testimony of Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, as well as the 92 ter witness statement of Marko Rajic and the complete trial transcript of his testimony." Did you receive those materials before you drafted the expert report or did you receive those materials after you drafted the expert report?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: My recollection is I received them after. I can -- I know that I didn't factor them into that initial report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you factor them into the addendum you later drafted?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I think I did consider Marko Rajic's, some of the information from his testimony, into the addendum. But I was in Santiago, Chile, when I wrote the addendum; I wasn't in the United States. I was there teaching a course and I didn't have the documents with me, and that report, that addendum is driven by facts and assumptions that are provided by counsel which I asked them to provide. That was the predominant source of information upon which I assessed each target. Now, I can't say that other information I saw at some point, I can't say absolutely it did not influence my assessment. But the -- the predominant source of information that I relied on were those facts and assumptions. I did remember a fact I thought was significant that I had learned, I believe, in the meeting in Tampa, and when I got the facts and assumptions, I remember it was a Skype call from Tampa to here, and I said, you know, I think this -- I've always thought this was a significant factor. And they said, If you think it's a significant factor, you can add that as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, as a former advocate yourself and you have obviously have significant experience in criminal trials, you do understand that one of the hallmarks of the reliability of an expert's report is the transparency in the sources relied upon by the expert to draw their conclusions; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if there were time considerations or logistical consideration with documentation that you didn't have at the time, I understand that. I just want to know why, if you couldn't do it at the time, why you didn't follow up later to specifically indicate which documents you relied upon for which portions of your addendum?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Well, for the addendum specifically, because I made a decision that I needed to make -- render that opinion based on the information that was -- had been presented to the Tribunal, and I felt the most efficient and logical way to do that would be to ask counsel to give me what they believed were the relevant facts and assumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, sorry to interrupt, but the witness in one of his previous answer referred to one specific fact he made a phone call about. Could you tell us what that fact was, what considered of such importance that you would verify whether you could use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, I'm sorry to interject, that was part of my next follow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll not -- you can already think about the question, but Mr. Russo will put some other questions to you. I thought you had left the area, but apparently not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge has hit on the -- what you just mentioned. It is also discussed in paragraph 9 of your supplemental information sheet where you point out that the assumption which we find at page 30, subparagraph (d) in your addendum, is it's an assumption that you made in the report but you recalled it from the meeting you had in Tampa. You gave the Gotovina Defence a call to either refresh their recollection or yours about that and find out if that was a defensible point that you could use in your analysis. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This is where my concern begins because, obviously, if you were confining your addendum only to the facts and assumptions which were provided to you in the May 19th letter, you wouldn't have had to call them to ask to add additional factors in there. So it's clear, at least to me, and please correct me if I'm wrong, that you also did, in fact, rely on the oral presentation during late December in drafting your addendum. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I don't think could I have written it without having that general concept of the operation in my mind. So yes. The answer your question is yes. I did rely on the overview of the operation, the general -- what we would call in military parlance the concept of the operation. But this was a specific fact related to the General's decision-making process. And before I allowed that to influence my opinion, I made a decision that I needed to validate that as consistent with the other facts and assumptions, was that one that was -- they were confident had been established in the record. And that's why I addressed that specific one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And knowing the concern for transparency in the report, why didn't you insist that the entire discussion that you had, at least all of the information that was provided to you and the documents shown to you, why didn't you insist that that be memorialised either as facts and assumptions or in some other way and attached to your addendum?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I mean, I don't know if I even contemplated that question. I know that what I wanted to do was to make sure that I was rendering an opinion that applied the standard of prospective critique properly. I didn't want to look at what happened and look back and say, In my opinion, because this happened, it was illegal. Because, as I stated in the first report, I think that is not the proper application of the legal standards that regulate combat operations as they're transformed into a source of criminal responsibility. And therefore, I felt it was critical for me to render this opinion that the opinion be based on facts and assumptions available to General Gotovina as revealed in the record -- the proceedings of the trial. So candidly, I -- I -- my expectation was I might have been given information that he wasn't aware of at the time. I don't think that's relevant in me critiquing his battlefield judgement at the time he makes a decision because I have to look at -- I have to apply the objective standard of the law through his subjective perception of the situation at the time, and that's what I asked the Defence to provide me. That was a decision, the decision not to engage those fleeing forces, that stood out in my mind, because it seemed quite significant. And when that was not in that list of facts and assumptions, I thought that it was something that I needed to raise, and that's why I addressed that one specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, you said: "I didn't want to look at what happened and look back and say, In my opinion, because this happened it was illegal." For the record, we find that at draft transcript page 85, lines 9 to 11. This sounds to me to be something of a limitation on the opinions you've offered. I want to see if I'm correct in that. First of all, there's a difference, you would agree, in what somebody tells you they knew at the time and what other people may find based on other evidence was, in fact, the situation at the time. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: There's a difference between direct and circumstantial evidence. If somebody tells me they saw it, it's direct evidence. If there's a fact that creates an inference, that's circumstantial evidence. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And for purposes of your addendum, you weren't -- am I right, you weren't interesting in hearing or looking at evidence of what happened and then determining whether -- what actually happened constituted a violation of the laws of armed conflict. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: No, I think that's overbroad. You look at effects because that is a source of circumstantial evidence from which can you infer certain conclusions. But what I was opposed to was looking at only effects and then considering facts that were unavailable to the defendant at the time he made his decision, and then concluding from that, that he made a flawed decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I want to take this sort of step by step. First of all, there's -- if you look at what actually happened, that can include evidence both of what General Gotovina claims to have known at the time, and also include evidence of what he should have known at the time. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Yes. Facts that were available to him at the time of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Right. And it's -- that's part of the concern I have with the alternate method you suggested by asking the Defence to provide you only with facts and assumptions that General Gotovina claims to have relied on. Wouldn't you agree with me that you're essentially closing your eyes to evidence that could have demonstrated to you what he should have known and should have relied on?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Well, I think that you're -- you're missing the distinction between facts and assumptions, okay? Facts are facts established that are established by the record related to the mission. Assumptions are assumptions that were made by the commander. They're both relevant in the decision-making process. I agree with you 100 per cent that you could have a situation where there was an objective fact that was available for the defendant that he ignored or failed in his duty to make himself aware of, and that would be relevant in assessing whether or not he discharged his responsibility in accordance with the law. But facts, some of the facts that were listed in that -- in the response to my request were facts related to effects. So I'm not suggesting that effects are not relevant. They're -- they're -- you can see that they talk about -- that the targets that were placed under fire, okay? If you change that fact, if you tell me that those targets were never placed under fire, that the only things placed under fire were hospitals, schools and civilian buildings, then it fundamentally alters the opinion. So the facts and assumptions, I think, certainly my expectation was that they were not simply what the Defence could tell me for certain the General knew. They were general facts related to the situation and then the commander's assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I do -- I understand that, Professor. What I'm putting to you is that the analysis that you conducted is based on -- on the methodology that you saw fit to employ necessarily not independent that by refusing to take a look -- an independent look at the evidence itself, you deprived yourself of the opportunity to find evidence which could either suggest to you that General Gotovina was acting in bad faith or that an assumption he made was not in accordance with the actual situation or was in some way disingenuous. How do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I think that is always a potential risk when you render an opinion, and my assumption is if there is a significant fact or assumption that I failed to make myself aware of, then that is part of the adversarial testing of the opinion and that you would have the opportunity to expose that to me and ask me if that would modify my opinion. So I would readily concede that for -- and for my opinion to be absolutely perfect, it would have been ideal to sit in this courtroom and listen to the entire case. It would have been even more ideal to sit in General Gotovina's command post in Croatia and monitor the decision-making process. There's no question that the degree of information you have enhances the foundation for the opinion you render, and -- and that's why I -- I was insistent with Defence counsel that they not give me what they ideally hoped would be the factual conclusions of the adversarial process or the trial process, but they give me facts and assumptions that they have a degree of confidence were established by the record. Now, I know that is not foolproof, and I know that the Prosecution certainly is likely to contest some of those facts and assumptions, but that's what I based the opinion on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation, Professor. I do understand you come from an adversarial system, as do many of the lawyers in the courtroom. I want to step back from this particular line of questioning so I want to just touch on this today before we move on. Looking at your curriculum vitae, which is Exhibit D1641, I notice on page 5, under the heading "International and National Security Law Experience," the second position you list there, chief, international law and operations division office of the Judge Advocate, US Army Europe, June 2001 to July of 2003, the third bullet point there indicates that you provide expert advice in support of all military lawyers involved in active operations throughout the Balkans. Can you give us a little explanation of the involvement you had in the Balkans at that time?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: The military lawyers that I advised were US military lawyers involved in operations in Bosnia and Kosovo. The IFOR mission in Bosnia, the US component of that mission, and the SFOR mission in Kosovo, the US component of that mission. I was not an advisor to NATO commands so I did not advise or provide assistance to the IFOR headquarters or the SFOR headquarters. But in both of those missions there was a large US contingent and those contingents had a strong presence of US military lawyers, and when they would get legal issues related to the planning and conduct of military operations that they felt they needed assistance on, that was the function of my office, was to provide that next level of expert assistance to them. And -- and I can tell you with fair -- a fair degree of certainty what the primary focus of that was. It was detention operations in Kosovo. That was the -- 90 per cent of our focus was dealing with those issues. Bosnia, by that point in time, had been -- become a relatively stable environment. And for whatever reason, the -- the US military legal officer in Bosnia was always senior to the officer in Kosovo. So there was always a colonel in Bosnia and usually a major in Kosovo, so the -- the qualification of the senior officer in Bosnia rendered the need for our involvement there less significant. The other area that caused a lot of challenge was fiscal law, what you're allowed to spend money on and what money you're allowed to execute the operation. Those were the two primary focus of our legal assistance to those missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Professor Corn, from the fact that we had to wait such a long time you may understand this to be an encouragement to further slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, at paragraph 12 of your supplemental information sheet, you list documents that you were provided with by the Gotovina Defence and you indicate this was subsequent to the drafting of your report. It's unclear to me, though, if you got them after the report and before the addendum, or if you got them after both the report and the addendum were drafted.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I know I did not consider any -- any of this when I wrote the initial report. I know I received a FedEx box with a number of documents in it. I think I received it before I wrote the addendum, although I am not positive. I know that when I wrote the addendum I was in Chile, and I didn't bring those documents with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can I take it from that answer that you did not specifically consider these documents in the drafting of your addendum?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: I mean, I think some were -- were copies of photographs that I had seen in the meeting in Tampa, so if they were related to the general concept it probably was something that I would have factored in. But, as a general proposition, that's an accurate statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Beyond this list we find in paragraph 12 and the oral presentation you were provided with at the end of December 2008, were there any other documents or pieces of information -- also, the testimony of Konings and Rajcic, with the exception of those, is there anything else that you were shown or told with respect to the substance of this case?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN
utterances.text: Well, I can't immediately correlate the number with the document. I can tell you other information that I have considered in my preparation to come over here. There was a transcript from a meeting between the president and members of the military staff, including the General; I think it was in Brioni. I looked at that. There were some psychological operations directives that I looked at related to information to influence the conduct of the civilian population. Rajcic's testimony was something that I looked at extensively. As I said, the visual disposition of military objectives in Knin was obviously something that was important, in my mind. So, I mean, that's a candid kind of offer of the -- of the information that I think had a significant influence on my thought process.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 13 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, this particular line of questioning may take more than a few minutes. I understand we only have a few left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have only a few left. Therefore, perhaps better start with that tomorrow. Yes. Is there any procedural matter anyone would like to raise at this moment because then we will see whether we need Professor Corn for it. If not, then we could use those five minutes for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We don't need Professor Corn for the procedural matter that I will address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Corn, we'd like to adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow morning, 9.00, in this same courtroom. But before I let you go I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone, whoever it is, about your testimony, whether testimony already given or still to be given. Madam Usher will escort you out of the courtroom and we'd like to see you back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. At this time the Gotovina Defence would like to make an ore tenus motion to withdraw the expert report of Mr. Pokaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to withdraw the application for admission into evidence of an expert report of Mr. Pokaz, so that Mr. Pokaz now is not part of the record anymore, apart from procedural history but not as far as the substance is concerned. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The only other matter is the issue that we briefly touched on this morning concerning the Rule 68 issue, and the only reason I raise that at this juncture, Mr. President, is I'm not sure exactly where that's going to take us with having to incorporate that additional information, either in a bar table submission or requesting, you know, to bring witnesses back or incorporating it in the witness that Mr. Misetic will address next week. I simply don't know. Given I do have the exhibit that was sent about last week by Mr. Misetic that was presented in the Popovic case that apparently had been extant in the records of the Office of the Prosecutor for some time. But given the fact that we are coming to the end of the Prosecution -- excuse me, the Defence case for General Gotovina, we certainly would like to see if we can incorporate or obtain this information to make the correct decisions as we move to the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps for the record, there is an issue of disclosure of -- from what I understood is an order preparing for operational activity issued by Mr. Mladic which dates from the early days of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 3 August, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3 of -- 3rd of August, and the issue is that the Defence considers this to be exculpatory evidence which should have disclosed, where they found it only recently on the public record in the Popovic case. Just to see whether I understood you well, Mr. Kehoe, you'll consider -- now it's on the record what we are talking about. You'll consider in which way you want to approach this matter procedurally and that we'll hear from you as soon as you have made up your mind, and that for the time being, it is just put on the record that there is a disclosure issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The further disclosure issue is this is an attack order from the 3rd where General Mladic orders an attack for 6.00 in the morning on the 5th. It is an operation that is called Vaganj, V-a-g-a-n-j, 95. And what we are looking for is the documents that are encompassed in this because there are any number of documents, and I will tell that it concerns not only this offensive that was planned by the VRS and General Mladic to kick off on the 5th. There are also some documents, it appears in the Popovic case, that detail the redeploying of units from the Drina Corps to fight the HV as early as the 9th of August in that area. So that's a series of items and we're just looking for as much as possible to see in fact what we're going to do with them and how we will proceed, if we will just bar table them or is there some other appropriate measure to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you have to further explore the matter of the context of it, other documents and then you will come back to the Chamber and tell us in which way you would like to proceed in relation to this. That is on the record. This being the case, Mr. Russo, I will not invite you at this moment to respond. Of course, if there's any useful communication possible between the parties on the issue, the parties are encouraged to use the opportunity to do so. We will adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, the 8th of September, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of September, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 25
